newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysian shares seen near rebound - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysian shares seen near rebound - analysts.

text.p: Malaysian share prices have likely bottomed out, but may trade within a tight range over the next two to six months even though corporate earnings and economic fundamentals remain sound, analysts and dealers said.
"The market has seen the worst of the current slump. There is reassuring support at the 1,060 level," said Ramlan Ahmad, senior manager at local fund managers Commerce MGI.
Stephen Weller, director of strategy at Pesaka Jardine Fleming, said: "The market will need one or two months to recuperate, and should trade within about two to three percent of current levels."
"We need to look through the sentiment and concentrate on the hard numbers," said Weller.
Those hard numbers translate to average corporate earnings growth of around 15 percent, and a market price-to-earnings ratio of around 14 times, said Weller.
Malaysian share prices have fallen around 14 percent since February 28, when the Kuala Lumpur Composite Index closed at 1,270.67. The blue-chip index fell to a nine-month low of 1,059.51 on April 29.

"We are now into around week 11 of the current down-cycle. The maximum length of a down-cycle over the last five years has been around 15 weeks, so we are nearing the end of that period," said a futures trader at a local brokerage house.
A number of events have helped depress share prices since late February.

On March 4 the then chairman and chief executive of national car maker Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional Bhd (Proton), Yahaya Ahmad, was killed, resulting in the suspension of nine listed companies linked to him and the DRB-Hicom group.
In mid-March a row between Malaysia and Singapore hit sentiment on both sides of the causeway.
A 25-basis point increase in U.S. interest rates in the same month sent Wall Street shares tumbling, which helped pull local share prices even lower.

But the nail in the coffin came on March 28 when Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara, imposed curbs on property and share lending in order to curb excessive speculation in these sectors. Property and banking stocks were the worst affected.
A series of sell programs by foreign institutional funds followed.
Even though several key blue-chip stocks are now trading far below their levels at the start of the year, fund managers and analysts are being selective in their choices of stocks to buy.

"We are looking at consumer stocks aimed at middle-income earners and companies with strong cash flows like Genting Bhd and Tanjong Plc," said Simon Maughan, head of research at brokers W.I. Carr in Kuala Lumpur.
Other sectors Maughan said were looking attractive at current levels were insurance, finance and telecommunications.
Wednesday's midday trade saw blue-chip share prices rise by around 1.4 percent to 1,104.90.
But sentiments continue to remain weak, analysts said.
"I would expect the market to trade within a five percent range of 1,100 for the next few months, and I don't think it will exceed 1,150 for the next three months," said Ramlan.
